--- title: "Model Evaluation: How Do We Know the Model Is Actually Good?" description: "A rigorous but intuitive guide to validation design, regression and classification metrics, thresholds, calibration, cross-validation, uncertainty, leakage and business-aware model evaluation." author: "MLStation" date: 2026-10-01 categories: [ML, Evaluation, Data Science] draft: false ---
🧪 Training asks: “Can the model learn?” Evaluation asks: “Can I trust what it learned?”
A model can achieve 99% accuracy and be useless. It can have excellent ROC-AUC and produce poor probabilities. It can dominate random cross-validation and fail next month. Evaluation is therefore a **design problem**, not merely a metric calculation.
# 1. The Fundamental Rule: Evaluate Unseen Data If model parameters are learned from $\mathcal D_{\text{train}}$, performance must be estimated on data not used to fit those parameters. ```text ALL DATA │ ├── TRAIN ── learn parameters │ ├── VALIDATION ── choose/tune │ └── TEST ── final unbiased-ish assessment ``` ::: {.callout-warning} ## The test set is not a development dashboard If you repeatedly inspect test performance and change the model, the test set becomes part of model development. ::: # 2. Simulate a Realistic Binary Classification Problem ::: {#ad40411b .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show simulated churn-data code"} import numpy as np, pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.datasets import make_classification from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split X,y=make_classification( n_samples=6000,n_features=12,n_informative=6, n_redundant=2,weights=[.86,.14], class_sep=1.0,flip_y=.025,random_state=42 ) X_train,X_test,y_train,y_test=train_test_split( X,y,test_size=.25,stratify=y,random_state=42 ) ``` ::: # 3. Always Build a Baseline For imbalanced classification, predicting the majority class may yield high accuracy. ::: {#4572e93f .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier dummy=DummyClassifier(strategy="prior") dummy.fit(X_train,y_train) print("Dummy accuracy:",dummy.score(X_test,y_test)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Dummy accuracy: 0.852 ``` ::: ::: Your model should beat a meaningful baseline—not merely produce a large-looking number. # 4. The Confusion Matrix For binary classification: | | Predicted − | Predicted + | |---|---:|---:| | Actual − | TN | FP | | Actual + | FN | TP | From these four counts, many recurring metrics emerge. # 5. Accuracy $$ \text{Accuracy}=\frac{TP+TN}{TP+TN+FP+FN}. $$ Useful when classes and error costs are reasonably balanced. Dangerous when the positive class is rare or errors have asymmetric cost. # 6. Precision and Recall $$ \text{Precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP} $$ asks: > Of the cases we flagged, how many were truly positive? $$ \text{Recall}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN} $$ asks: > Of all true positives, how many did we catch? ### Use-case intuition **Fraud investigation with limited analysts:** precision matters. **Cancer screening where missing a case is costly:** recall can matter strongly. Neither metric should be selected without the decision context. # 7. F1 Score $$ F_1= 2\frac{\text{Precision}\cdot\text{Recall}} {\text{Precision}+\text{Recall}}. $$ F1 is a harmonic mean and is useful when you want one number balancing precision and recall. But one number hides the tradeoff. # 8. Thresholds Turn Scores into Decisions A classifier may produce a probability-like score $p$. Decision: $$ \hat y= \begin{cases} 1,&p\ge t\\ 0,&p=t).astype(int) rows.append({ "threshold":t, "precision":precision_score(y_test,pred,zero_division=0), "recall":recall_score(y_test,pred,zero_division=0), "f1":f1_score(y_test,pred,zero_division=0) }) threshold_df=pd.DataFrame(rows) ``` ::: ::: {#72f38088 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} import plotly.express as px long=threshold_df.melt("threshold",var_name="metric",value_name="score") fig=px.line(long,x="threshold",y="score",color="metric", markers=True,title="Threshold changes the operating point") fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: :::
### Model selection and decision selection are different First learn a scoring/ranking model. Then choose an operating threshold based on costs, capacity, risk and product objectives.
# 9. ROC Curve and ROC-AUC ROC plots $$ TPR \quad \text{vs.}\quad FPR $$ over thresholds. AUC measures ranking discrimination: how well positives tend to receive higher scores than negatives. ::: {#2fe38f2b .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve,roc_auc_score fpr,tpr,_=roc_curve(y_test,prob) auc=roc_auc_score(y_test,prob) fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5,5)) ax.plot(fpr,tpr,label=f"AUC={auc:.3f}") ax.plot([0,1],[0,1],linestyle="--") ax.set(xlabel="False Positive Rate",ylabel="True Positive Rate", title="ROC curve") ax.legend() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](evaluation_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){width=734 height=750} ::: ::: # 10. Precision–Recall Curve For rare positive classes, PR curves often expose the useful operating region more directly. ::: {#a6cbb9bc .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve,average_precision_score precision,recall,_=precision_recall_curve(y_test,prob) ap=average_precision_score(y_test,prob) fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5,5)) ax.plot(recall,precision,label=f"AP={ap:.3f}") ax.set(xlabel="Recall",ylabel="Precision",title="Precision–Recall curve") ax.legend() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](evaluation_files/figure-html/cell-7-output-1.png){width=734 height=750} ::: ::: # 11. Log Loss — Reward Honest Probabilities For binary classification: $$ -\frac1n\sum_i [y_i\log p_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)]. $$ Confident wrong predictions are punished strongly. Use when probability quality matters, not merely hard labels. # 12. Calibration — Does 0.8 Mean About 80%? A calibrated model satisfies approximately: $$ P(Y=1\mid \hat p\approx0.8)\approx0.8. $$ ::: {#577019de .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} from sklearn.calibration import calibration_curve obs,pred=calibration_curve(y_test,prob,n_bins=10) fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5,5)) ax.plot(pred,obs,marker="o") ax.plot([0,1],[0,1],linestyle="--") ax.set(xlabel="Predicted probability",ylabel="Observed rate", title="Calibration") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](evaluation_files/figure-html/cell-8-output-1.png){width=734 height=750} ::: ::: Ranking and calibration are separate properties. # 13. Regression Metrics Suppose residuals are $$ e_i=y_i-\hat y_i. $$ ## MAE $$ MAE=\frac1n\sum|e_i|. $$ Easy to interpret in target units and less dominated by large errors than MSE. ## MSE $$ MSE=\frac1n\sum e_i^2. $$ Large errors receive quadratic penalty. ## RMSE $$ RMSE=\sqrt{MSE}. $$ Returns the error to target units. ## $R^2$ $$ R^2=1-\frac{\sum(y_i-\hat y_i)^2} {\sum(y_i-\bar y)^2}. $$ Measures improvement relative to predicting the mean under the usual definition. # 14. Simulate Why MAE and RMSE Tell Different Stories ::: {#24521fd0 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} rng=np.random.default_rng(8) errors=rng.normal(0,10,500) errors[:5]=[60,-75,90,-110,130] mae=np.mean(np.abs(errors)) rmse=np.sqrt(np.mean(errors**2)) print("MAE :",round(mae,2)) print("RMSE:",round(rmse,2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` MAE : 8.89 RMSE: 13.89 ``` ::: ::: RMSE reacts much more strongly to rare large misses. That can be desirable if large misses are disproportionately costly. # 15. Residual Diagnostics A single regression metric cannot tell you *how* a model is wrong. Plot residuals against: - predictions, - important features, - time, - customer segments. Look for: - bias, - nonlinear pattern, - changing variance, - segment-specific failure, - temporal drift. # 16. Cross-Validation A single split can be lucky or unlucky. $K$-fold CV: ```text Fold 1: VALID | train train train train Fold 2: train | VALID | train train train Fold 3: train train | VALID | train train ... ``` ::: {#e993daba .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} from sklearn.model_selection import cross_validate scores=cross_validate( LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), X,y, cv=5, scoring=["roc_auc","average_precision","neg_log_loss"] ) pd.DataFrame(scores).filter(like="test_").describe() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Report variation, not only the mean. # 17. Choose the Split That Matches Reality ## IID rows Random K-fold may be appropriate. ## Imbalanced classification Use stratification. ## Multiple rows per person/device/account Use grouped splitting to prevent entity leakage. ## Future prediction Use time-ordered validation.
### The split is part of the model A sophisticated metric on an unrealistic split produces a sophisticated-looking wrong answer.
# 18. Interactive Cross-Validation Variability ::: {#9dfc1472 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show repeated split simulation"} from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold,cross_val_score vals=[] for seed in range(15): cv=StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5,shuffle=True,random_state=seed) s=cross_val_score( LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), X,y,cv=cv,scoring="roc_auc" ) vals += [{"seed":seed,"fold":i+1,"auc":v} for i,v in enumerate(s)] cv_df=pd.DataFrame(vals) ``` ::: ::: {#55ed41d5 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} fig=px.scatter(cv_df,x="seed",y="auc",color="fold", title="Performance varies across validation samples") fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: # 19. Hyperparameter Tuning Without Cheating Hyperparameters are selected using training/validation information. Examples: - regularization strength, - tree depth, - number of trees, - learning rate, - neighborhood size. Tools include: - grid search, - randomized search, - successive halving, - Bayesian/optimization frameworks such as Optuna. Never tune repeatedly on the final test set. # 20. Learning Curves — More Data or Better Model? Plot training and validation performance against training-set size. Interpretation: ```text train high, validation low → overfitting / variance problem both low → underfitting / bias or weak features validation still improving with n → more data may help ``` # 21. Validation Curves — What Does Complexity Do? Vary one hyperparameter and compare train vs validation scores. Example: tree depth. ```text depth too small → underfit depth moderate → useful region depth huge → training perfect, validation deteriorates ``` # 22. Confidence Intervals and Bootstrap A metric is an estimate from a finite sample. Bootstrap evaluation: ```text test rows ↓ sample with replacement metric₁ repeat B times ↓ distribution of metric ↓ uncertainty interval ``` ::: {#3258839a .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} rng=np.random.default_rng(99) boots=[] idx=np.arange(len(y_test)) for _ in range(1000): b=rng.choice(idx,size=len(idx),replace=True) if len(np.unique(y_test[b]))==2: boots.append(roc_auc_score(y_test[b],prob[b])) print(np.quantile(boots,[.025,.5,.975])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [0.82901722 0.85677176 0.88489216] ``` ::: ::: # 23. Segment Evaluation Overall performance can hide failures. Evaluate by: - region, - device, - customer tier, - acquisition channel, - time period, - operationally meaningful cohorts. A model can have excellent aggregate AUC while performing poorly on a strategically important subgroup. # 24. Business Evaluation Suppose: - TP saves $120, - FP costs $15, - FN loses $200. Then a threshold can be evaluated by expected value, not only F1. $$ V(t)=120TP(t)-15FP(t)-200FN(t). $$
### Metrics are proxies for decisions The best statistical metric is not automatically the best business operating point.
# 25. Offline vs Online Evaluation Offline: - historical holdout, - CV, - metrics, - calibration, - slices. Online: - A/B experiment, - latency, - engagement, - revenue, - guardrails, - operational load. A model that wins offline still needs evidence that it improves the real system. # 26. Monitoring After Deployment Evaluation does not end at launch. Monitor: - input drift, - prediction distribution, - missingness, - calibration, - delayed ground-truth performance, - latency/errors, - business KPI, - subgroup behavior. # 27. The Evaluation Ladder
BASELINE → SPLIT → METRICS → THRESHOLD → DIAGNOSTICS → CROSS-VALIDATE → UNCERTAINTY → SEGMENTS → BUSINESS VALUE → ONLINE TEST → MONITOR
# Summary A trustworthy evaluation answers more than “What is the score?” Ask: 1. **Compared with what baseline?** 2. **On what unseen population?** 3. **Using which metric and why?** 4. **At which threshold?** 5. **How uncertain is the estimate?** 6. **Does it hold across folds, time and segments?** 7. **Does it improve the real decision?** 8. **Will we know when performance changes?**
